Action Policy is a Ruby library that helps you decide who is allowed to do what in your application. This guide introduces its core ideas so you can add authorization to a Ruby or Ruby on Rails project. Authorization is the process of determining whether a given user is permitted to perform a given action on a given resource, such as viewing, editing, or deleting a record. It is distinct from authentication, which establishes who the user is; authorization assumes the user is already known and asks what that user may do.


The central concept in Action Policy is the policy class. A policy class is an ordinary Ruby class that describes the access rules for a single kind of resource. The recommended convention is to create one policy per resource and name it after the model with a Policy suffix, so that a Post model is governed by a PostPolicy; in Rails these classes live in the app/policies folder. Within a policy, each rule is a public method whose name is the predicate form of an action, such as show? or update?, returning true when the action is permitted and false when it is not. Rules must be public, since private methods raise an error. It is common to define an ApplicationPolicy base class that holds shared configuration and to have other policies inherit from it.

Inside a rule you have access to two values that Action Policy provides automatically. The first, called user, is the subject performing the action, by default the currently authenticated user. The second, called record, is the target object being acted upon. A rule combines these to reach its decision; an update rule might permit the change only when the user is an administrator or owns the record.

Once policies are defined, you enforce them by calling a method that checks the relevant rule. When the rule returns true, execution continues normally; when it returns false, Action Policy raises an unauthorized error you can rescue and handle. Action Policy can usually infer which policy and rule to apply from the resource and action name, while still letting you name them explicitly when needed.

This section explains how to build a custom base policy in Action Policy, a Ruby authorization library, so that you understand what a policy class is composed of and how to replace the default building blocks. In Action Policy, a policy is an ordinary Ruby class that holds the rules deciding whether a given user is permitted to perform a particular action on a particular record. Each rule is a predicate method, a method whose name ends in a question mark and that returns true or false. Applications conventionally place these rules in a shared parent class named ApplicationPolicy, from which all individual policies inherit.

By default, that parent class inherits from ActionPolicy::Base, which is a ready-made combination of every available policy extension assembled with sensible default configuration. ActionPolicy::Base brings together a set of modules, each contributing one capability: a core module that performs the actual authorization checks, along with separate modules that add pre-checks, human-readable failure reasons, rule aliases, scoping of collections, caching of results, and a set of default rules. When used with Ruby on Rails, it also registers scope matchers for ActiveRecord relations and for controller parameters, and it enables instrumentation through Active Support notifications. The defaults it supplies include treating the current user as the authorization subject, using a general manage? rule as the fallback, aliasing the new? action to create?, and denying the index?, create?, and manage? actions unless you override them.

You are not required to inherit from this fully featured base. If the bundled defaults do not fit your needs, you can write ApplicationPolicy from scratch and include only the pieces you actually want. The single indispensable component is the core module, ActionPolicy::Policy::Core, which provides the fundamental apply and allowed_to? methods that every policy relies on to evaluate rules. A minimal policy therefore needs nothing more than that one module included in your class.

One caveat applies when working with Rails: the custom scope matchers that let policies filter ActiveRecord relations and controller parameters are normally registered inside ActionPolicy::Base. If you build your own base instead, you must copy that setup code yourself in order to keep using those matchers.

TestProf is a toolbox for profiling and optimizing automated tests written in Ruby. This overview explains what the project does, why the performance of a test suite is worth caring about, and the kinds of tools the toolbox provides to diagnose and fix slow tests.

To understand TestProf, it helps to define a few terms. A test suite is the full collection of automated tests that a project runs to verify that its code behaves correctly. Profiling is the practice of measuring where a program spends its time, so that the slowest parts, often called bottlenecks, can be identified and addressed. A profiler is a tool that performs this measurement. TestProf brings these ideas together for Ruby, giving developers a way to see which tests, and which operations inside those tests, consume the most time.

The performance of a test suite matters for two practical reasons. First, running tests is part of a developer's everyday feedback loop: after changing code, a developer typically runs the tests to confirm nothing broke, so a slow suite delays that feedback and interrupts concentration. Second, tests are usually run again as part of the deployment process, before new code reaches production, so slow tests lengthen the time between finishing work and shipping it. In short, slow tests waste time and reduce productivity, and TestProf exists to help recover that time.

Rather than being a single tool, TestProf is a collection of related ones. It offers ready-to-use integration with general-purpose Ruby profilers such as ruby-prof and stackprof, so they can be pointed at a test suite with little setup. It includes analyzers and profilers focused on object factories, which are a common and frequently overlooked source of slowness, along with profilers built on ActiveSupport instrumentation. It also provides helpers for the popular RSpec and Minitest frameworks that make individual tests faster, and a set of RuboCop rules to support good practices.

TestProf is widely adopted in the Ruby community, used by large projects to meaningfully reduce how long their test suites take to run, which demonstrates that careful profiling can yield substantial, measurable improvements.

This guide explains the let_it_be recipe from TestProf, a Ruby toolkit for profiling and speeding up test suites, and shows how it helps you set up shared test data with very little effort. Many automated tests need example records in the database before they can run. In the RSpec testing framework, the usual way to create such records is with the let and let! helpers, which define a named value for each test. The trouble is that let! recreates its records before every single example, so a group of twenty tests that all rely on the same four records will build those four records twenty times over. For test suites that touch a real database, this repeated setup is one of the most common reasons tests run slowly.

To understand let_it_be, it helps to first understand before_all, another TestProf feature. The before_all helper runs a block once for an entire group of related tests rather than once per test, wrapping the whole group in a database transaction that is rolled back afterward. This makes the setup data repeatable across examples while creating it only one time. The drawback is that before_all forces you to assign your records to instance variables and to define them all together in a single block, which makes it awkward to adopt in existing tests that already use let and let!.

The let_it_be helper combines the convenience of let with the efficiency of before_all. You write let_it_be exactly as you would write let!, giving each record a name and a block that creates it, but the record is created only once for the surrounding group of tests instead of once per example. In practice, converting a slow test file can be as simple as replacing each let! with let_it_be. One important detail follows from this design: let_it_be restores the database between groups of tests but not between individual examples within a group. You therefore still need a mechanism that wraps each example in its own transaction and rolls it back, such as transactional fixtures in RSpec Rails, the DatabaseCleaner gem, or equivalent custom setup, so that one test does not leak data into the next.

This guide explains how to install AnyCable, run its server, and connect a client to it, so that you can begin building real-time features for your application. AnyCable is a real-time server: a long-running program that maintains persistent connections with many web clients at once and pushes messages to them instantly, rather than requiring each client to repeatedly ask for updates. It is written in the Go programming language and described as language-agnostic, meaning that although it integrates closely with Ruby applications, it is not tied to any single programming language on the application side. Its design emphasizes performance and reliability when handling large numbers of simultaneous connections.

The server component is called anycable-go. The most direct way to obtain it is to download a pre-compiled binary, a ready-to-run executable that requires no compilation on your machine. On macOS the binary can be installed through the Homebrew package manager, and on Arch Linux it is available through the AUR. For JavaScript and TypeScript projects, AnyCable-Go can also be installed as an NPM package, in which case the matching server binary is downloaded automatically the first time the command runs. Once installed, the server is started simply by running anycable-go, after which it prints startup information and begins listening for connections.

A central idea behind AnyCable is that the server itself contains no business logic. It acts as a proxy that forwards work to a separate backend, which authenticates connections, authorizes subscriptions, and processes incoming messages. By default the server expects this backend to be a gRPC server, a remote procedure call service, listening on localhost port 50051, which is the standard location used by the companion Ruby library. For situations that only need publish and subscribe messaging, AnyCable can instead run in a standalone mode without any backend, using token-based authentication and signed message streams to control access. Clients communicate with the server using the Action Cable protocol, and an official JavaScript client library is provided so that web applications can subscribe to channels and exchange messages with the server.

This article explains how three approaches to running WebSocket servers behave under real production conditions, so that you can choose between them for a Node.js, TypeScript, Bun, or Deno application. A WebSocket is a persistent, two-way connection between a browser and a server that stays open so either side can send messages at any moment, which is what makes real-time features such as chat, live updates, streaming responses from language models, and collaborative editing possible. Because that connection is long-lived, the cost and reliability of holding many of them at once becomes the central engineering question.

The three options compared here represent different philosophies. Socket.io is a widely used JavaScript library that wraps WebSockets and adds conveniences such as automatic reconnection and rooms for grouping connections; it can optionally enable connection state recovery, a feature that briefly buffers messages so a client that drops offline can receive what it missed. uWebSockets.js is a lower-level library focused on raw speed and a minimal memory footprint, exposing a built-in publish and subscribe interface but leaving recovery and observability to the developer. AnyCable is a separate process, written in Go, that your application broadcasts to over HTTP; it handles the connections itself and includes a message broker, and it comes in a free open-source edition and a commercial Pro edition that packs connections more densely in memory and shares replay state.

To compare them fairly, each option runs as a standalone WebSocket service on identical hardware, an apples-to-apples setup that is reproducible from an open benchmark repository. The measurements fall into a few plain questions. Latency asks how quickly a message makes a round trip, reported as typical and worst-case times across ten thousand connections. Reliability asks what fraction of messages survive an unstable network with intermittent drops. Reconnect behavior asks whether the server stays healthy when an application deploy forces every client to reconnect at once. Footprint asks how much memory each idle connection consumes, which determines how many a single machine can hold and therefore what the system costs to run at scale.

This tutorial teaches you how to build a GraphQL application using Ruby on Rails on the backend and React with Apollo on the frontend, starting from nothing and finishing with your first working query. By the end you will understand what GraphQL is, why developers reach for it, and where it can lead you astray, so that you can decide whether it suits your own project rather than adopting it simply because it is popular. GraphQL appears everywhere now, but there is no silver bullet, and it is worth understanding both its advantages and its trade-offs before shifting an existing application away from REST.

GraphQL is, according to its specification, both a query language and a runtime, also called an execution engine. A query language is a way of describing how a client communicates with an information system: it defines the form of the requests a client can make. The runtime is the part responsible for fulfilling those requests by gathering and returning the actual data. At the heart of every GraphQL application sits a schema, which describes the underlying data as a directed graph, meaning a set of types connected by relationships. The runtime must answer queries according to this schema, so any valid GraphQL server processes the same query against the same schema in the same way and returns data in the same format. In effect, the schema is everything a client needs to know about the API.

A query selects a portion of that schema. It names the fields it wants, starting from a root field, and may pass arguments such as an identifier to locate a specific record. Because a query mirrors a sub-graph of the schema, a client can request exactly the data it needs, no more and no less, in a single round trip. This directly addresses overfetching, a common frustration with traditional REST APIs where endpoints often return more information than the caller wants. GraphQL schemas are also strongly typed, which means both the client and the runtime can verify that the data exchanged matches the declared types, catching mistakes early and making the contract between frontend and backend explicit and reliable.

This tutorial explains the N+1 query problem in Ruby on Rails: what it is, why it slows applications down, and how to detect and prevent it. By the end of the introduction you will understand the pattern, see how Rails lets you avoid it, and know which tools help you catch it before it reaches production.

It helps to define a few terms first. Ruby on Rails is a web framework whose database layer, ActiveRecord, maps database tables to Ruby objects and lets one record reference related records through associations. A message can belong to a user, and a user can have many messages. When you load a collection of records and then, for each one, access an associated record, ActiveRecord may issue one query to fetch the collection and then a separate query for every single item in it. This is the N+1 query problem: one query to load N records, plus N more to load the associations, for a total of N+1 trips to the database. It is a common performance anti-pattern, because each round trip carries overhead, and many small queries are far slower than one well-formed query.

A short illustration makes this concrete. Suppose you fetch three messages and then print the name of the user who sent each one. Rails runs one query for the three messages, then three more, one per message, to look up each user. That is four queries where two would suffice, and this inefficient communication takes a real toll on performance as data grows.

The basic solution is straightforward: you tell ActiveRecord to eagerly preload the associated records, so it gathers all the related users in a single additional query rather than one per record. That reduces the work to two queries regardless of how many messages you load.

Simple as the fix is, N+1 queries are stubborn in real, long-lived projects. The pattern behaves like the mythical Hydra, regrowing a head the moment a developer looks away. To keep it under control, you need proper instrumentation. The sections that follow introduce the tools that give you that sword and fire: the bullet gem, ActiveSupport instrumentation, and rspec-sqlimit.

This article explains how to set up a Docker-based development environment for Ruby and Ruby on Rails projects, an approach the author and his colleagues call "Ruby on Whales." Ruby on Rails is a popular web application framework written in the Ruby programming language, and like most software projects, a Rails application depends on many supporting pieces: a specific version of the language itself, a database such as PostgreSQL, a JavaScript runtime such as Node.js, and various system libraries. Getting all of these installed correctly on each developer's machine is often tedious and error-prone, and small differences between machines lead to the familiar complaint that code "works on my machine" yet fails elsewhere.

The central idea here is the reproducible development environment, meaning a setup that behaves identically for every person working on a project, regardless of the operating system or tools already installed on their computer. A reproducible environment makes it far easier to bring new engineers onto a team, to let non-engineers spin up a project, and to roll out changes to shared infrastructure such as databases and native dependencies without each person having to reconfigure their own machine by hand.

The common way to achieve this today is containerization. A container is a lightweight, isolated package that bundles an application together with everything it needs to run, so the same dependencies are present everywhere the container is launched. Containers can run on a developer's own laptop through tools like Docker or Podman, or remotely through services such as Codespaces, Coder, and Gitpod. A project's dependencies can be placed in a single container, or split across several containers in a multi-service architecture where the application, the database, and other services each run separately and communicate with one another.

Ruby on Whales applies these ideas specifically to Ruby on Rails. It is a local development configuration built around Docker, using a multi-service architecture managed through Docker Compose, the tool that coordinates several containers as one system. The author arrived at this configuration over several years, beginning with heavier virtual machines before moving to containers in 2017, and the sections that follow explain how the setup works and the reasoning behind its choices.

This article explains how to find and fix the parts of a Ruby or Rails test suite that make it slow, using a profiling tool called TestProf. To follow along, it helps to understand a few terms. A test suite is the full collection of automated tests that a project runs to check that its code behaves correctly. In the Ruby and Rails world, writing such tests is a normal and valued part of development, so most applications accumulate hundreds or thousands of them over time. Profiling means measuring where a program spends its time, so that effort to speed things up can be aimed at the slowest parts rather than guessed at. TestProf, then, is a profiling toolbox built specifically for tests: instead of telling you how fast your application serves users, it tells you which tests are slow and why, so you can shorten the time you spend waiting for results.

The reason this matters becomes clear once a suite grows large. A small set of tests finishes in seconds, but a suite with thousands of tests can take many minutes to run from start to finish. Every minute spent watching a suite run is a minute a developer is not writing code, and that delay repeats many times a day. Survey data gathered from Ruby developers shows the effect of scale directly. Among all test suites, the slowdown looks modest: only about a quarter run longer than ten minutes, and roughly half finish in under five. But once you narrow the view to suites with more than a thousand tests, the picture changes sharply. About half of those larger suites take more than ten minutes, and nearly thirty percent take more than twenty. Typical production Rails applications often hold ten to twenty thousand tests, placing them firmly in that slower group.

You rarely run an entire suite for every small change; during ordinary work on a feature you might run only a hundred or so examples before a commit. Even so, the full suite still runs regularly, and when it drags it quietly drains productivity. The chapters that follow show how to measure that cost precisely and bring it down.

This piece explains how to judge whether a software technology has lasting value rather than fleeting popularity, using the web framework Ruby on Rails as its central example. The goal is to give a general reader a way of thinking about any new framework, programming language, or tool that promises to change how software is built, so that excitement and skepticism alike can be weighed against evidence.

A few terms are worth defining first. A software framework is a reusable foundation of code and conventions that handles common tasks, letting developers build applications faster than they could from scratch. Ruby on Rails, usually shortened to Rails, is one such framework, first released in 2005, that became popular for building web applications quickly. The phrase "hype cycle" refers to the predictable pattern by which a new technology attracts enthusiasm, then disappointment, before its real worth becomes clear. The research firm Gartner formalized this pattern into a model called the Gartner Hype Cycle, which divides a technology's life into five phases: a technology trigger that creates initial buzz, a peak of inflated expectations driven by early publicity, a trough of disillusionment as reality falls short of the excitement, a slope of enlightenment as practical uses emerge, and finally a plateau of productivity built on proven value.

Understanding this cycle matters because the moment a technology is most celebrated is often the moment it has proven the least. When a tool is new and trending, it is not yet a mature technology; it is a promise, a hypothesis about what might be built. Real technology is the accumulated result of years of work by many people, including the authors and maintainers who create it and, crucially, the users who integrate it into real workflows. The meaningful test comes after the enthusiasm fades: are people still choosing the technology for pragmatic reasons, still investing their time, money, and effort in it and its ecosystem, even when it is no longer fashionable? Rails moved through every phase of this cycle, including a period when it was widely declared dead, and its later resurgence shows what survival on genuine value actually looks like.

This report explains what early-stage venture funding looked like for developer-focused startups between January 2025 and March 2026, and what the companies that raised money actually did to earn it. To understand it, a few terms help. Developer tools, often shortened to devtools, are products built for software engineers rather than for general consumers: code editors, deployment platforms, testing services, and similar infrastructure. A funding round is an event in which a startup sells ownership stakes to investors in exchange for cash, and rounds are named by stage. The earliest is pre-seed, followed by seed, then Series A and Series B, each typically larger than the last as a company proves more of its business. Venture capital firms, abbreviated VCs, are the investment funds that supply much of this money. The analysis covers 1,140 such rounds across developer tools, cybersecurity, and infrastructure, drawn from a raw Crunchbase export of 1,206 deals after removing roughly 60 companies that do not sell to developers.

The piece sets out to answer two practical questions. The first is descriptive: how much money flowed, into which categories, and at what typical size per stage. Over the fifteen-month window these rounds totaled about $13.5 billion. Roughly half of the deals involved artificial intelligence, about half involved cybersecurity, and a fifth touched both, while the companies tied to neither still grew under the broader influence of AI. At every stage beyond pre-seed, AI companies tended to raise larger rounds than their peers.

The second question is explanatory: rather than stopping at the numbers, the report studies how about 130 funded companies actually grew, reconstructing their paths from founder interviews, podcast appearances, and press coverage to identify the specific product decisions and go-to-market tactics that drew investment. It also maps the most active investors by category, naming individual partners, so a founder knows whom to approach for a given kind of product. One caveat frames everything that follows: Crunchbase data is incomplete, since some rounds go unreported or are reported late, so the figures should be read as directional rather than exact.
